title: Directing a Project in Context

header.html: 4.2.1 carry out directing a project: activities, inputs and outputs; recommended roles and responsibilities; how the practices are applied; 4.2.2 analyze whether the activities, roles and responsibilities are effective and fit for purpose, using the purpose and objectives, the practices and tailoring

toc.title: The board's decisions, inputs and outputs

html:
1Purpose, objectives and context

The directing a project process lets the project board be accountable for the project's success. The board makes the key decisions and keeps overall control, and it delegates day-to-day management to the project manager. The process runs from the end of start-up until closure. It is not a stage and not a single event.

In plain words, the objectives are:

  • Authority to initiate, deliver and close is given at the right points.
  • The board has the information it needs and control at every decision point.
  • Management gets timely direction and advice when it asks.
  • Closure is authorized and follow-on actions are arranged.

The process serves manage by exception (the board steps in only at decision points or on an exception), manage by stages, ensure continued business justification, define roles, responsibilities and relationships and tailor to suit the project.

Exam tip

. Directing is the board's process and it spans the whole project. The project manager does not direct; the project manager manages within the limits the board sets.

2The board's decisions, inputs and outputs

The decision names below are in general terms. Learn what the board decides and with which products.

Decision The board mainly uses The board gives
Authorize initiation Project brief; initiation stage plan Authority to initiate the project
Authorize the project PID; plan for the next stage Authority to deliver; baselines accepted; resources committed
Authorize a stage or exception plan End stage report; next stage plan, or exception report and exception plan Authority for the stage, with its tolerances
Give ad hoc direction Highlight reports; issue reports; requests for advice; outside events Decisions and guidance for the project manager
Authorize project closure End project report; lessons report; evidence of acceptance; follow-on action recommendations Closure authorized and follow-on actions accepted

Between these points the board manages by exception. The project manager works within the stage tolerances, and the board reads highlight reports and acts when asked or when an exception is reported. The board can also decide to close the project early if it is no longer justified.

Exam tip

. Work in a stage starts only when the board has authorized the stage. If a project manager starts the next stage before the board's decision, the approach is not appropriate.

3Roles and responsibilities

The board is a team, but one person is accountable overall. Learn each focus and check the Official Book's responsibility table.

Role Focus in directing
Executive Accountable for the project; chairs the board; owns the business case and its continued justification
Senior user Makes sure the products meet user needs; commits user resources; answers for benefits
Senior supplier Commits supplier resources; answers for the quality and feasibility of supplier work
Project manager Supports the board with information, plans and requests for decisions; does not take board decisions
Project assurance Gives the board independent checks, so decisions rest on reliable information
Project support Administers board papers, meetings and records
Change authority Decides on changes within delegated limits, so the board does not have to
Corporate or programme management Sets the project tolerances; receives escalation beyond them
Exam tip

. The executive is accountable; the three board roles decide together; the project manager informs but does not decide for the board. In a "who" question, an answer that moves a board decision to the project manager or to assurance is wrong.

4How the practices are applied

Practice Applied in directing
Business case Checks justification at every decision point; stops the project if it no longer holds
Organization Board in place with all three interests; authority delegated to the project manager
Plans Approves the project plan baseline and each stage plan; asks for an exception plan when needed
Quality Satisfied that the quality approach is sound; confirms acceptance at closure
Risk Approves the risk approach; takes risks escalated to it
Issues Decides issues beyond the project manager's authority; sets up the change authority and any change budget
Progress Sets stage tolerances; reads highlight reports; responds to exception reports
Exam tip

. The board delegates by tolerance. Anything the project manager can decide within the stage tolerances should not be brought to the board.

5Judging the process

What effective directing looks like Red flag, with the principle
Decisions at the right points, with enough information Next stage approved with no business case review (business justification)
Routine work delegated within tolerances The board approves minor day-to-day choices (manage by exception)
Ad hoc direction given quickly when asked Board members unavailable, so work waits for weeks (manage by stages)
The board does not manage the stage The board gives instructions to team members (define roles)
All three interests have a voice The executive decides alone, or the supplier dominates (define roles)
The board stops an unjustified project Work continues to avoid embarrassment (business justification)
Independent information supports decisions The board relies only on the project manager's view (define roles)

Tailoring changes how the board works, not what it decides.

Setting How directing changes
Small project A short board; decisions by email or a brief call; roles combined only where independence and accountability stay clear
Agile or hybrid delivery The board authorizes stages or releases; the product owner can speak for the user interest; sprints are managed inside the stage
Large or multi-party project Formal minutes and tighter links with the corporate or programme level
Sustainability and digital concerns Sustainability targets reviewed at decisions; electronic sign-off and shared dashboards
Exam tip

. If a board decides too little, projects drift; if it decides too much, it stops managing by exception. Look for a board that decides at decision points, delegates the rest and answers quickly when asked.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1During Project Harbor's build stage, which is within tolerance, Sam Okafor, the project manager, asks the board to approve swapping two developers between work packages. Was this an appropriate action, and why?

  • AYes, because the board is accountable for every resourcing choice made during the stage
  • BYes, because the senior supplier must approve any change to the supplier's own team
  • CNo, because Sam can decide this within the stage tolerances and keep the board for exceptions
  • DNo, because the change authority, not the project board, decides on resource swaps in a stage
Show the answer

Answer: C. Manage by exception means the project manager decides routine matters within tolerance, and the change authority deals with changes to baselines, not resource swaps.

S2Sam has finished the end stage report and the next stage plan for Project Harbor's pilot stage, and Aisha Bello has checked them. Who makes the decision to authorize the rollout stage?

  • AThe project board, meeting at the stage boundary
  • BThe project manager, who wrote the report and plan
  • CProject assurance, who checked the information
  • DThe change authority, who holds delegated authority
Show the answer

Answer: A. The board authorizes each stage, while the project manager and project assurance provide and check the information.

S3At the end of Project Harbor's initiation stage, the board must decide whether to authorize the project. Which products does it mainly use?

  • AThe project brief and the plan for the initiation stage
  • BThe end stage report and the exception plan
  • CThe end project report and the lessons report
  • DThe PID and the plan for the first delivery stage
Show the answer

Answer: D. Authorizing the project rests on the PID and the next stage plan, while the brief and initiation stage plan support the earlier decision to initiate.

S4Tomas Reyes, the senior user, cannot attend the board meeting that decides on Project Harbor's rollout stage next week and has nominated nobody. What should Sam do?

  • AAuthorize the rollout stage himself so that the plan is not delayed any further
  • BRaise the gap with Marta Quinn so someone with authority covers the user role
  • CAsk Wei Chen to speak for the harbor users at the board meeting on Tomas's behalf
  • DAsk Aisha Bello to take the senior user decision, as she provides project assurance
Show the answer

Answer: B. The user interest must be represented with authority at the decision, and the project manager cannot take the board's decision or fill the role alone.

S5A small internal Brightwater project has a board of three that meets at each stage end and reads a short highlight report by email between meetings. Was this an appropriate way to direct the project, and why?

  • ANo, because every board must meet each month, whatever the size or risk of the project
  • BNo, because highlight reports must be discussed in a meeting and not sent by email
  • CYes, because small projects need no board decisions between initiation and closure
  • DYes, because the board kept its decision points and used light controls between them
Show the answer

Answer: D. Tailoring lightens the board's working methods while keeping its decisions at the decision points and management by exception between them.

S6Delta Software delivers Project Harbor's build stage in two-week sprints. Marta Quinn asks Sam to bring each sprint plan to a board meeting for approval. Was this an appropriate action, and why?

  • ANo, because the board authorizes the stage and leaves sprints to the project manager
  • BNo, because agile teams do not need board authority at any point in the project
  • CYes, because the executive must approve every plan produced by the team during a stage
  • DYes, because the senior supplier must confirm every sprint that the supplier's team staffs
Show the answer

Answer: A. The board authorizes the stage and sets tolerances, while sprint planning sits inside the stage under the project manager's authority.

6.2 Recall questions

R1What is the purpose of directing a project?

Show the answer

To let the board be accountable by making key decisions and keeping overall control while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager.

R2Name the board's five main decisions.

Show the answer

Authorize initiation, authorize the project, authorize a stage or exception plan, give ad hoc direction and authorize project closure.

R3Who is ultimately accountable on the project board?

Show the answer

The executive.

R4What does manage by exception mean for the board between decision points?

Show the answer

The board lets the project manager work within tolerances and acts on highlight and exception reports.

R5Which report prompts the board to consider asking for an exception plan?

Show the answer

The exception report.

R6When does directing a project run?

Show the answer

From the end of start-up until closure.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Purpose board accountable; key decisions and overall control; day-to-day delegated
Decisions initiation, the project, a stage or exception plan, ad hoc direction, closure
Inputs brief, PID, stage plans, reports, closure information
Roles executive accountable; senior user and senior supplier; project manager informs
Between decisions manage by exception within stage tolerances
Red flags too much detail, slow decisions, a board that manages the stage
Tailoring lighter methods, same decisions
